To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ERG expression is heterogeneous in most patients and that the heterogeneity increases with tumor size.
ERG expression is heterogeneously distributed in the prostate and in the individual prostate cancer.
the vast majority of prostate cancers are heterogeneous for ERG expression, and that ERG expression is more frequent in young patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the development and progression of prostate cancer.
the development of novel therapies for the treatment of cancer and other diseases.
the identification of new biomarkers for the detection of prostate cancer and its progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ERG fusions are frequent, heterogeneous and early in prostate cancer.
the vast majority of cancers have TMPRSS2:ERg fusions but that these fusions are not present in all cancer cells of the same tumor focus.
ERG fusions are frequent, but not constant during prostate cancer progression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TMPRSS2-ERG fusions are common in young men and occur in 50 % or more of prostate cancer cases.
the ERG fusion is a common event in prostate cancer, but it is not a driver for the development of prostate cancer.
the majority of prostate cancers have TMPRSS2-ERG fusions and these fusions are not restricted to the primary tumor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ERG status of a cancer focus should not be used to classify patients into ERG fusion positive and negative prostate cancer, but rather should be considered an independent prognostic parameter.
ERG expression in early-onset and elderly prostate cancer is not a binary phenomenon, and ERG expression should be assessed in all cancer foci of a given patient.
the ERG fusion is an important event in prostate cancer progression, but it does not define the entire tumor.
